answer.rationale: The 18% mandate creates strong pull toward switch_primary_vendor, but memory_c2 attaches an explicit constraint to exactly that move: the low-cost vendor missed delivery SLA in three of four quarters and must not be sole source on a critical line. With the line at 94% of committed volume and zero buffer, a primary-vendor switch inside 14 days converts a cost problem into a delivery-failure problem. So the cost target has to be met on the incumbent relationship rather than by replacing it. memory_c4 says renegotiation at renewal recovered real margin when benchmarked against market rates, and memory_c6 says multi-year commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing service scope; the low-cost vendor's quoted pricing from memory_c2 is usable as benchmark leverage even though we will not award them the line. memory_c1 supports that staying with the incumbent avoids migration work at a moment when we cannot absorb interruption. I verify memory_c4 because it is the load-bearing claim for my chosen action (if the recovered margin was small or one-off, negotiation alone will not reach 18% and I need to know that before committing), and memory_c2 because it is the one memory whose caveat is blocking the otherwise-obvious cost move and I want the original record's magnitudes and dates before relying on it that heavily. Deliberately not verifying memory_c3, memory_c5, memory_c6: add_second_source is the right structural answer to concentration risk but not deliverable in 14 days with one decision slot, and defer_decision fails because this contract does not auto-renew, so deferral means lapse rather than month-to-month continuity as in memory_c5. Uncertainty I am carrying forward and not resolving: whether negotiation actually closes the full 18% gap, and whether memory_c2's cost advantage still holds at current market rates. If negotiation lands short, the next-cycle move is add_second_source with the low-cost vendor on a bounded non-critical share, not a primary switch. Downstream risk flagged: a later agent reading memory_c2's cost headline under budget pressure could easily drop the SLA caveat and award them the critical line; the caveat and the 94%/no-buffer context must travel together with any cost figure I record, and any negotiated savings I book should not be written as evidence that the incumbent is cheapest absent the benchmark that produced it.
